en: Rough and bad-mannered; rude and insensitive
hook: BOORISH: like a BOAR (wild pig) at the dinner table.
story: At the fancy restaurant, one guest talked loudly on his phone, chewed with his mouth open, and snapped his fingers at the waiters. Other diners glared at his boorish behavior. Boorish means crude and ill-mannered, like a wild boar at a dinner party. A boor has no sense of social grace.

en: To tolerate or allow (usually used in the negative)
hook: GRE trick: BROOK isn't just a stream. 'She brooks no nonsense' means she TOLERATES none.
story: The new headmistress brooked no excuses for lateness. Five minutes late meant waiting outside until the break, whether you were a student or a teacher. To brook means to tolerate, and it almost always appears with 'no' or 'not'. The GRE loves this word because everyone thinks it only means a small stream.

en: Cautious; carefully considering all circumstances before acting
hook: CIRCUM-SPECT: looking (spect) all around (circum) before acting.
story: Before signing the lease, Nadia was circumspect: she read every clause, checked the landlord's references, and inspected every pipe and wire. She didn't want any surprises. Circumspect means cautious and careful, looking around at all possible risks before acting. A circumspect diplomat chooses every word carefully.

en: Courteous and considerate behavior; mutual respect between groups or nations
hook: COMITY looks like COMMUNITY: people living in harmony.
story: Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists, and Christians in the old neighborhood celebrated each other's festivals, sharing sweets during Eid, Puja, and Christmas. This comity had lasted for generations. Comity means friendly mutual respect between groups or nations. Don't confuse it with comedy.

en: Corresponding in size, degree, or amount; proportionate
hook: COM-MEASURE-ate: of the same MEASURE.
story: Arif worked eighty hours a week, but his salary was not commensurate with his effort; he was paid as if he worked half that. He asked for a raise commensurate with his responsibilities. Commensurate means in proportion. A punishment should be commensurate with the crime.

en: Warm, friendly, and polite
hook: CORDIAL: from the HEART (cor, as in cardiac).
story: Although the two companies were competitors, their CEOs shared a cordial relationship. They greeted each other warmly, exchanged New Year's gifts, and even played golf together. Cordial means warm and friendly but polite. A cordial invitation is a sincere, heartfelt one.

en: Causing harm or damage
hook: DELETE-rious: it DELETES your health.
story: Doctors warned that the arsenic in some village tube wells was deleterious to health, causing skin lesions, cancer, and slow poisoning over years. Deleterious means harmful. Smoking has deleterious effects on the lungs; sleepless nights have deleterious effects on memory.

en: A division or contrast between two opposing things
hook: DI-CHOTOMY: cutting in two (di = two, tomy = cut).
story: The movie showed a sharp dichotomy between two Dhakas: glittering towers in Gulshan and crowded slums just across the lake. Rich and poor, side by side. A dichotomy is a division into two contrasting parts. GRE passages often discuss false dichotomies, such as 'either science or art.'

en: To instruct or improve someone morally or intellectually
hook: EDIFY: builds you up like an EDIFICE (building).
story: Grandfather's evening stories were meant not just to entertain but to edify. Each tale taught honesty, patience, or kindness. Edify means to improve someone's mind or character. An edifying documentary teaches you something valuable; a reality show usually doesn't.

en: Well chosen or suited to the situation; pleasing and fortunate
hook: FELICITOUS: FELICITY = happiness. A happily perfect choice.
story: At the farewell party, Mitu quoted a Tagore line about journeys and new beginnings. It was so felicitous, perfectly suited to the moment, that the departing teacher wiped away tears. Felicitous means apt and well-timed. A felicitous phrase fits perfectly; a felicitous coincidence brings happiness.

en: Having or showing great knowledge gained from study
hook: ERUDITE: 'E-READ-ITE', someone who has read everything.
story: Professor Rahman was erudite. He could discuss Bengali poetry, Greek philosophy, quantum physics, and Mughal architecture all in one conversation, quoting books from memory. Erudite means highly learned and scholarly. An erudite essay is full of deep knowledge.

en: Very fertile; capable of producing abundantly; intellectually productive
hook: FECUND: FERTILE and fruitful; produces a FECUND harvest.
story: The silt left by Bangladesh's rivers makes the delta among the most fecund lands on earth, producing three rice crops a year. Fecund means very fertile. It's also used for minds: a fecund imagination produces endless creative ideas.

en: Lacking physical strength; weak and unconvincing
hook: FEEBLE: sounds weak, like a FEEBLE 'meh'.
story: After a week of high fever, Tanvir's grandfather was too feeble to lift a glass of water. When Tanvir missed his deadline, he offered a feeble excuse: 'My dog ate my laptop.' Feeble means weak, physically or in quality. A feeble attempt barely tries.

en: To refrain from doing something; to hold back
hook: FOR-BEAR: BEAR (endure) it FOR now, and hold yourself back.
story: Sara wanted to tell her rude aunt exactly what she thought, but she forbore, smiling politely for the sake of family peace. To forbear is to hold yourself back from doing or saying something. Don't confuse it with forebear, which means an ancestor.

en: Lacking order or plan; random
hook: HAP-HAZARD: by HAPpenstance and HAZARD, by chance.
story: Rafi studied in a haphazard way: a few words from group nine, then some geometry, then an essay, then back to group two. No schedule, no pattern. His progress was just as random. Haphazard means lacking order or planning. Haphazard construction leads to unsafe buildings.

en: A confused mixture of different things
hook: HODGEPODGE: in Bangla, it's literally a 'khichuri' of things.
story: Arif's bedroom was a hodgepodge: old cricket bats, a broken guitar, GRE books, a fish tank with no fish, and twelve unmatched socks. A hodgepodge is a jumbled mix of unrelated things, like a messy khichuri where everything is thrown together.

en: To slow down or block progress
hook: IM-PEDE: 'ped' is foot. Something catching your feet.
story: Heavy rain, flooded streets, and a broken-down bus impeded Mitu's journey to the exam center. She arrived just in time. To impede is to obstruct or hinder. An impediment is an obstacle, like a speech impediment that makes talking difficult.

en: Acting quickly without careful thought
hook: IMPETUOUS: full of IMPETUS (sudden force), no brakes.
story: During a heated argument with his boss, the impetuous young engineer shouted, 'I quit!' and walked out. By evening, he regretted it deeply. Impetuous means acting on impulse without thinking. Impetuous decisions made in anger are usually bad ones.

en: Easily angered; hot-tempered
hook: IRASCIBLE: quick to IRE (anger).
story: The old shopkeeper was irascible. Ask a question twice and he'd shout; touch a product without buying and he'd snap at you. Even children avoided his shop. Irascible means easily provoked to anger. It's a synonym of irritable and short-tempered.

en: Motivated only by money; a soldier hired to fight for a foreign army
hook: MERCENARY: works only for MERCHANDISE and money.
story: The doctor recommended unnecessary tests and surgeries to every patient, just to charge higher fees. His patients realized he was mercenary, caring more about money than health. Mercenary means motivated purely by money. Historically, mercenaries were soldiers hired to fight for whoever paid them.

en: Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise
hook: METICULOUS: METIC-ulous, every metric measured perfectly.
story: Nadia's notes were meticulous: color-coded, neatly underlined, with every definition, synonym, and example sentence perfectly organized. Classmates borrowed them before every exam. Meticulous means extremely careful about details. A meticulous surgeon leaves nothing to chance.

en: Sharply sarcastic or critical
hook: MORDANT: it BITES (Latin mordere, to bite).
story: The comedian's mordant humor targeted politicians mercilessly. Every joke had a bite that left the audience laughing and wincing at the same time. Mordant means sharply biting and sarcastic. It's a synonym of caustic. A mordant critic's reviews can sting for years.

en: To move faster than; to exceed or surpass
hook: OUT-STRIP: running OUT ahead on the race STRIP.
story: In the last year, demand for electric bikes in Dhaka outstripped supply; shops had waiting lists of three months. To outstrip is to exceed or surpass. A brilliant student may quickly outstrip her teachers. When spending outstrips income, debt follows.

en: Dangerously unstable or uncertain
hook: PRECARIOUS: like a CAR parked on the edge of a cliff.
story: The construction worker stood on a bamboo scaffold six floors up, balancing on a single pole without a harness. His position was precarious. One slip, and he would fall. Precarious means dangerously insecure. A precarious job could disappear any day.

en: Having unusual or peculiar habits or features
hook: QUIRKY: full of QUIRKS, odd little habits.
story: Mitu's quirky roommate ate rice with a spoon, named all her plants after famous scientists, and only studied while standing on one leg. She was strange in a charming way. Quirky means unconventional and peculiar. A quirky café might have books hanging from the ceiling.

en: To refuse to accept or be associated with; to reject
hook: REPUDIATE: REPEL and DENY.
story: When the old video of him saying offensive things surfaced, the politician publicly repudiated his past views, calling them wrong and shameful. To repudiate is to reject something completely, refusing to accept or be associated with it. A government may repudiate a debt, refusing to pay it.

en: Skill in dealing with people without offending them
hook: TACT: a gentle TACTILE touch with words.
story: When her friend asked if her new haircut looked good, Sara used tact: 'It's a bold look! The color suits you.' She didn't lie, but she didn't hurt her friend either. Tact is sensitivity in handling difficult situations. Tactless people say whatever they think, without care.

en: Unimportant or trivial
hook: TRIFLE: a small, unimportant thing.
story: The shopkeeper and the customer argued for twenty minutes over a trifling sum: two taka. Both wasted far more in time and energy than the money was worth. Trifling means of little value or importance, a synonym of trivial. Don't let trifling matters distract you from real goals.

en: Characterized by conflict, disorder, or violent movement
hook: TURBULENT: like airplane TURBULENCE, shaking and chaotic.
story: The flight over the Bay of Bengal was turbulent; the plane shook, cups spilled, and passengers gripped their seats. The 1970s were a turbulent decade in the region's history, full of war and upheaval. Turbulent means violently disturbed, whether air, water, or times.
